description: Health of the PostgreSQL/TimescaleDB instance behind Perfana, sampled into monitoring.pg_samples by TimescaleDB background jobs.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  max(value) AS "Connections"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric = 'conn.total' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

panels.title: Connections in use
panels.description: Backends in use. max_connections differs per deployment, so the warning colours live on the percentage panel beside this one rather than on absolute counts here.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  100.0 * max(value) FILTER (WHERE metric = 'conn.total')
       / NULLIF(max(value) FILTER (WHERE metric = 'conn.max'), 0) AS "Used"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric IN ('conn.total', 'conn.max') AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

panels.title: Connection budget used
panels.description:
Backends against max_connections.

**When it crosses:** the pools reserve far more than they use — api 20, grafana-sync 10, the JMeter listener 20, the worker up to 30, against a handful actually running a query. Check *Connections by application* for the biggest reserver. Either raise max_connections in docker-compose.yml, or put the load generators behind PgBouncer so a fleet maps onto a bounded set of backends instead of a pool each.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  detail AS state,
  max(value) AS "connections"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric = 'conn.state' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;

panels.title: Connections by state
panels.description: idle in transaction is the one to watch: it pins a connection and holds back vacuum.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  source AS application,
  max(value) AS "connections"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric = 'conn.state' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;

panels.title: Connections by application
panels.description: Requires the services to set PGAPPNAME. Perfana's worker runs two pools on purpose -- 30 connections for analytics, 8 dedicated to writes -- after analytics was found starving writes; this is where that shows.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  source AS lock_mode,
  max(value) AS "waiting"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric = 'lock.waiting' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;

panels.title: Sessions waiting on a lock
panels.description: Empty is healthy: no rows are written when nothing is blocked.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  'oldest transaction — ' || source AS series,
  max(value) AS "seconds"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric = 'conn.xact_age_s' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;

SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  'idle in transaction — ' || source AS series,
  max(value) AS "seconds"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric = 'conn.idle_in_xact_age_s' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;

panels.title: Oldest transaction / query age
panels.description:
ADAPT analysis legitimately runs for minutes, so a long transaction is not by itself a fault. A long *idle* one is. 

**When it crosses:** Identify it with `SELECT pid, state, now()-xact_start AS age, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL ORDER BY age DESC`. A long *idle* transaction is a leaked connection: the worker pool sets idleTimeoutMillis to 600000, so anything older is not being recycled. A long *active* one is usually ADAPT and needs nothing.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  100.0 * sum(d) FILTER (WHERE metric = 'db.blks_hit')
        / NULLIF(sum(d), 0) AS "Hit ratio"
FROM (
  SELECT ts, metric,
    GREATEST(value - LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts), 0) AS d
  FROM monitoring.pg_samples
  WHERE metric IN ('db.blks_hit', 'db.blks_read') AND $__timeFilter(ts)
) x
WHERE d IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

panels.title: Cache hit ratio
panels.description:
Shared buffer hits as a share of all block reads. A sustained dip means the working set no longer fits in shared_buffers. 

**When it crosses:** shared_buffers is 4 GB. A batch re-evaluate on 2026-09-02 still dipped to 24% here with that in place, which buffer size no longer explains — at that point it is a query reading far more than it returns, not a cache that is too small. Catch it with pg_stat_statements ordered by shared_blks_read, then EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). Check the Storage row first — a dip right after a hypertable jump is a cold cache, not a misconfiguration.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  avg(rate) AS "commits"
FROM (
  SELECT ts, source,
    GREATEST(value - LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts), 0)
    / GREATEST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts))), 1) AS rate
  FROM monitoring.pg_samples
  WHERE metric = 'db.xact_commit' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
) r
WHERE rate IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  avg(rate) AS "rollbacks"
FROM (
  SELECT ts, source,
    GREATEST(value - LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts), 0)
    / GREATEST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts))), 1) AS rate
  FROM monitoring.pg_samples
  WHERE metric = 'db.xact_rollback' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
) r
WHERE rate IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  avg(rate) AS "inserted"
FROM (
  SELECT ts, source,
    GREATEST(value - LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts), 0)
    / GREATEST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts))), 1) AS rate
  FROM monitoring.pg_samples
  WHERE metric = 'db.tup_inserted' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
) r
WHERE rate IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  avg(rate) AS "updated"
FROM (
  SELECT ts, source,
    GREATEST(value - LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts), 0)
    / GREATEST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts))), 1) AS rate
  FROM monitoring.pg_samples
  WHERE metric = 'db.tup_updated' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
) r
WHERE rate IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  avg(rate) AS "deleted"
FROM (
  SELECT ts, source,
    GREATEST(value - LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts), 0)
    / GREATEST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts))), 1) AS rate
  FROM monitoring.pg_samples
  WHERE metric = 'db.tup_deleted' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
) r
WHERE rate IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  avg(rate) AS "fetched"
FROM (
  SELECT ts, source,
    GREATEST(value - LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts), 0)
    / GREATEST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts))), 1) AS rate
  FROM monitoring.pg_samples
  WHERE metric = 'db.tup_fetched' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
) r
WHERE rate IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

panels.title: Tuples per second
panels.description: Inserts dominate during a load test: every sampler result from every generator lands in requests_raw.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  avg(rate) AS "temp bytes/s"
FROM (
  SELECT ts, source,
    GREATEST(value - LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts), 0)
    / GREATEST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts))), 1) AS rate
  FROM monitoring.pg_samples
  WHERE metric = 'db.temp_bytes' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
) r
WHERE rate IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  avg(rate) AS "deadlocks/s"
FROM (
  SELECT ts, source,
    GREATEST(value - LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts), 0)
    / GREATEST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts))), 1) AS rate
  FROM monitoring.pg_samples
  WHERE metric = 'db.deadlocks' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
) r
WHERE rate IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

panels.title: Temp files and deadlocks
panels.description:
Temp bytes mean a query spilled past work_mem to disk. 

**When it crosses:** work_mem is 32 MB. That took the worst spill of a batch re-evaluate from 2.0 MB/s to 540 KB/s, so what remains is a single query still exceeding it. It applies per sort per connection, so multiply by the ~45 backends actually in use before raising it again. Deadlocks are unrelated: any non-zero rate is a bug to chase in the logs.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  avg(rate) AS "WAL bytes/s"
FROM (
  SELECT ts, source,
    GREATEST(value - LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts), 0)
    / GREATEST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts))), 1) AS rate
  FROM monitoring.pg_samples
  WHERE metric = 'wal.lsn_bytes' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
) r
WHERE rate IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

panels.title: WAL generated per second
panels.description: Derived from the LSN, so it counts everything written to the log. The clearest single signal of how hard a running test is hitting the database.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  max(value) AS "pg_wal size"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric = 'wal.dir_bytes' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

panels.title: WAL directory size
panels.description:
Growth here without a matching checkpoint rate means WAL is being retained -- a stalled archive, a replication slot, or max_wal_size too small. 

**When it crosses:** max_wal_size is 8 GB, so pg_wal settling near 8-9 GB is expected and 12 GB is not. Check `SELECT * FROM pg_replication_slots WHERE NOT active` first — an inactive slot pins WAL indefinitely. Otherwise raise max_wal_size, which also brings down the requested checkpoints beside it.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  max(value) AS "segments"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric = 'wal.dir_files' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  avg(rate) AS "timed"
FROM (
  SELECT ts, source,
    GREATEST(value - LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts), 0)
    / GREATEST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts))), 1) AS rate
  FROM monitoring.pg_samples
  WHERE metric = 'bgw.checkpoints_timed' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
) r
WHERE rate IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  avg(rate) AS "requested"
FROM (
  SELECT ts, source,
    GREATEST(value - LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts), 0)
    / GREATEST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts))), 1) AS rate
  FROM monitoring.pg_samples
  WHERE metric = 'bgw.checkpoints_req' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
) r
WHERE rate IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

panels.title: Checkpoints per second
panels.description:
Requested checkpoints are driven by WAL volume rather than by checkpoint_timeout. A rising share of them means max_wal_size is too small for the write rate. 

**When it crosses:** checkpoint_timeout is 300 s, so timed checkpoints arrive at 0.0033/s — the first threshold line. Once *requested* reaches it, WAL volume rather than the clock is driving checkpoints and each one competes with the ingest. Raise max_wal_size (8 GB now) until requested falls back to near zero.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  avg(rate) AS "by checkpointer"
FROM (
  SELECT ts, source,
    GREATEST(value - LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts), 0)
    / GREATEST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts))), 1) AS rate
  FROM monitoring.pg_samples
  WHERE metric = 'bgw.buffers_checkpoint' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
) r
WHERE rate IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  avg(rate) AS "by bgwriter"
FROM (
  SELECT ts, source,
    GREATEST(value - LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts), 0)
    / GREATEST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts))), 1) AS rate
  FROM monitoring.pg_samples
  WHERE metric = 'bgw.buffers_clean' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
) r
WHERE rate IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  avg(rate) AS "by backends"
FROM (
  SELECT ts, source,
    GREATEST(value - LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts), 0)
    / GREATEST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts))), 1) AS rate
  FROM monitoring.pg_samples
  WHERE metric = 'bgw.buffers_backend' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
) r
WHERE rate IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

panels.title: Buffers written per second
panels.description:
Backends writing their own buffers is the expensive path: it means the bgwriter and checkpointer are not keeping up. 

**When it crosses:** Read the threshold against the *by backends* line only; the other two are meant to be busy. shared_buffers is 4 GB and bgwriter_lru_maxpages is 1000 (from 100), because a 3-hour ingest test on 2026-09-03 had the cleaner pinned at its old 500/s ceiling while backends flushed 1000-3300/s themselves. If this line is high again, the cleaner ceiling is 20000/s now, so the answer is shared_buffers or the write rate, not the cleaner. Sustained backend writes during a run surface as latency in the load test itself.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  source AS "Job",
  -- Counters are cumulative, so difference them over the selected range: the table
  -- answers "what happened in the window I am looking at", not "since the job existed".
  max(value) FILTER (WHERE metric = 'job.total_runs')
    - min(value) FILTER (WHERE metric = 'job.total_runs')        AS "Runs",
  max(value) FILTER (WHERE metric = 'job.total_successes')
    - min(value) FILTER (WHERE metric = 'job.total_successes')   AS "Successes",
  max(value) FILTER (WHERE metric = 'job.total_failures')
    - min(value) FILTER (WHERE metric = 'job.total_failures')    AS "Failures",
  max(value) FILTER (WHERE metric = 'job.last_duration_s')       AS "Last duration (s)",
  max(value) FILTER (WHERE metric = 'job.age_since_success_s')   AS "Since success (s)"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric LIKE 'job.%' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 4 DESC, 1;

panels.title: Background jobs
panels.description:
The continuous aggregate refresh policies behind every Perfana dashboard, plus the retention and columnstore policies. A refresh that stops succeeding shows up as stale dashboards long before it shows up as an error. Counts are for the selected time range.

**When Failures is non-zero:** read the reason with `SELECT err_message, count(*) FROM timescaledb_information.job_errors GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC`. "failed to start job" means no background worker was free — compare Worker processes beside this table: max_worker_processes must exceed timescaledb.max_background_workers plus max_parallel_workers. Anything else is a real query error and the message names it. *Since success* is the staleness of that aggregate: while it climbs, the Perfana dashboards reading it are behind.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  max(value) FILTER (WHERE metric = 'worker.jobs_registered')          AS "jobs registered",
  max(value) FILTER (WHERE metric = 'worker.timescaledb_processes')    AS "TimescaleDB processes",
  max(value) FILTER (WHERE metric = 'worker.timescaledb_max_background') AS "timescaledb max",
  max(value) FILTER (WHERE metric = 'worker.max_worker_processes')     AS "max_worker_processes"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric LIKE 'worker.%' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

panels.title: Worker processes
panels.description: The budget, not the instantaneous load: a continuous aggregate refresh finishes in tens of milliseconds, so counting workers in flight would read zero almost always. Saturation shows up as failures in the Background jobs table. max_worker_processes must exceed timescaledb.max_background_workers plus max_parallel_workers, or jobs lose the race for a worker.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  max(value) AS "database"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric = 'db.size_bytes' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  source AS hypertable,
  max(value) AS "bytes"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric = 'hypertable.bytes' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;

panels.title: Hypertable size
panels.description: The result tables grow with every test run; this is what fills the disk on a long-lived deployment.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  source AS "table",
  100.0 * max(value) FILTER (WHERE metric = 'table.dead_tup')
       / NULLIF(max(value) FILTER (WHERE metric = 'table.live_tup'), 0) AS "dead %"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric IN ('table.dead_tup', 'table.live_tup') AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1, 2
HAVING max(value) FILTER (WHERE metric = 'table.dead_tup') > 0
ORDER BY 1, 2;

panels.title: Dead tuples
panels.description:
Dead tuples as a share of live ones — the absolute count says nothing without the table size. The result tables are insert-only, so this should stay low. 

**When it crosses:** autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor is 0.2, so autovacuum should fire at 20% — the first threshold line is exactly where it ought to have run already. Check `SELECT relname, last_autovacuum, autovacuum_count FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC`. A stale last_autovacuum usually means a long-lived transaction is holding the xmin horizon back — see *Oldest transaction age*. Otherwise lower autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor for that table.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  source AS queue,
  max(value) AS "waiting"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric = 'queue.wait' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;

panels.title: Jobs waiting
panels.description:
Backlog per queue. perfana-analyze is the one that matters during a test run: it carries the analysis pipeline. 

**When it crosses:** A spike straight after starting a batch is normal — watch whether it drains. If it holds while *Jobs active* sits flat at its ceiling, the workers are the limit: raise WORKER_ANALYZE_CONCURRENCY / WORKER_BATCH_CONCURRENCY. If active is below its ceiling as well, the workers are blocked on the database — look at Connections and Temp files.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  source AS queue,
  max(value) AS "active"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric = 'queue.active' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;

panels.title: Jobs active
panels.description: Bounded by the worker concurrency settings, so a flat ceiling here next to a rising backlog means the workers are the bottleneck, not Redis.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  'failed — ' || source AS series,
  max(value) AS "jobs"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric = 'queue.failed' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;

SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  'delayed — ' || source AS series,
  max(value) AS "jobs"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric = 'queue.delayed' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;

panels.title: Jobs failed and delayed
panels.description:
Delayed jobs are usually retries with backoff, so a rising delayed count tends to precede a rising failed count. 

**When it crosses:** Failed jobs do not retry once attempts are exhausted. Read the reason with `valkey-cli LRANGE bull:<queue>:failed 0 10`, then find that job id in the worker log. A rising *delayed* count on its own is retries in flight and often clears itself.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  source,
  avg(rate) AS "completed/s"
FROM (
  SELECT ts, source,
    GREATEST(value - LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY source ORDER BY ts), 0)
    / GREATEST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY source ORDER BY ts))), 1) AS rate
  FROM monitoring.pg_samples
  WHERE metric = 'queue.completed' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
) r
WHERE rate IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;

panels.title: Jobs completed per second
panels.description: Throughput of the pipeline. BullMQ trims the completed set, so this is a rate of the retained window rather than of all time.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  max(value) AS "connected clients"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric = 'redis.connected_clients' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  max(value) AS "blocked clients"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric = 'redis.blocked_clients' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  max(value) AS "ops/s"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric = 'redis.instantaneous_ops_per_sec' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

panels.title: Valkey clients and operations
panels.description: Blocked clients are workers parked in BRPOPLPUSH waiting for a job — a healthy idle state, not a stall.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  max(value) AS "used"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric = 'redis.used_memory' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  max(value) AS "rss"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric = 'redis.used_memory_rss' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  max(value) AS "peak"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric = 'redis.used_memory_peak' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

panels.title: Valkey memory
panels.description:
maxmemory is 0 (unlimited) by default, so growth here is bounded by the host, not by Valkey. 

**When it crosses:** BullMQ trims its completed and failed sets, so steady growth means something is not being trimmed — usually a queue with no worker consuming it. Compare with Jobs waiting per queue to find which, and `valkey-cli --bigkeys` to name the key.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  100.0 * sum(d) FILTER (WHERE metric = 'redis.keyspace_hits')
        / NULLIF(sum(d), 0) AS "Hit ratio"
FROM (
  SELECT ts, metric,
    GREATEST(value - LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts), 0) AS d
  FROM monitoring.pg_samples
  WHERE metric IN ('redis.keyspace_hits', 'redis.keyspace_misses') AND $__timeFilter(ts)
) x
WHERE d IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  source,
  max(value) AS "keys"
FROM monitoring.pg_samples
WHERE metric = 'redis.keys' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;

SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  avg(rate) AS "evicted/s"
FROM (
  SELECT ts, source,
    GREATEST(value - LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts), 0)
    / GREATEST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts))), 1) AS rate
  FROM monitoring.pg_samples
  WHERE metric = 'redis.evicted_keys' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
) r
WHERE rate IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

SELECT
  time_bucket('$__interval', ts) AS time,
  avg(rate) AS "expired/s"
FROM (
  SELECT ts, source,
    GREATEST(value - LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts), 0)
    / GREATEST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY ts))), 1) AS rate
  FROM monitoring.pg_samples
  WHERE metric = 'redis.expired_keys' AND $__timeFilter(ts)
) r
WHERE rate IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

panels.title: Keys, evictions and expiries
panels.description:
Evictions are the alarming one: with maxmemory unset they should stay at zero, and a non-zero rate means jobs are being dropped. 

**When it crosses:** An eviction means Valkey dropped a key to stay under maxmemory, and a dropped BullMQ key is a lost job. Check `valkey-cli CONFIG GET maxmemory`: if something set it, raise it or give the container more memory. Expiries are normal and need no action.

title: PostgreSQL health
